en: Itivuttaka 59: Tikanipāta, Paṭhamavagga Thus it was said. This is the fifty-ninth discourse in the Third Chapter of the First Division. "Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a heap of filth, the person who is like a lotus, and the person who is like a diamond. And what, monks, is the person who is like a heap of filth? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a low family—a family of outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, cartwrights, or flower-pressers—one that is poor, with little food and drink, lacking sustenance, where it is difficult to subsist, and where one must struggle to live. He is moreover ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored; he has a repulsive appearance, is deformed, and is afflicted by many diseases: he suffers from jaundice, consumption, epilepsy, leprosy, boils, eczema, tuberculosis, or dysentery. He is short-lived, often meets with untimely death, and is frequently afflicted by suffering, sorrow, and despair. This, monks, is called the person who is like a heap of filth. And what, monks, is the person who is like a lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family—a family of kshatriyas, brahmins, or householders—one that is wealthy, with abundant food and drink, well-provided with sustenance, where one does not have to struggle to subsist, and where one lives in comfort.

He is handsome, beautiful, and fair-complexioned; he is pleasing to look upon, possesses a lovely form, and is free from disease. He is long-lived, rarely meets with untimely death, and is seldom afflicted by suffering, sorrow, and despair. This, monks, is called the person who is like a lotus. And what, monks, is the person who is like a diamond? Here, monks, a certain person is reborn in a high family—a family of kshatriyas, brahmins, or householders—one that is wealthy, with abundant food and drink, well-provided with sustenance, where one does not have to struggle to subsist, and where one lives in comfort. He is handsome, beautiful, and fair-complexioned; he is pleasing to look upon, possesses a lovely form, and is free from disease. He is long-lived, rarely meets with untimely death, and is seldom afflicted by suffering, sorrow, and despair. Having thus been reborn in a high family, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness. Having gone forth, he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha; possessed of right conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking and following the training rules. Having thus become restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, he dwells with sense-doors guarded, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension, and endowed with a mind that is collected and untroubled regarding the mental objects that arise through the six bases of contact. Having thus become restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha and possessing sense-doors that are guarded, he becomes moderate in eating; reflecting wisely, he takes his food neither for amusement nor for intoxication, nor for the sake of physical beauty and charm, but only for the support and maintenance of this body, for its preservation, for the ending of discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, thinking: ‘Thus I shall terminate the old feeling and not give rise to a new feeling. Having thus become moderate in eating, he devotes himself to wakefulness; during the day, while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. During the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot resting upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having set up mindfulness before him. During the last watch of the night, rising up, while walking back and forth and sitting, he purifies his mind of obstructive states. Having thus devoted himself to wakefulness, he applies himself to the development of concentration; secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which is internal composure and mental unification, free from thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is beyond pleasure and pain, and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness. When his concentrated mind is thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge and vision of the destruction of the taints. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. Through his understanding of things as they really are, through his higher knowledge of them, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of existence, and from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. This, monks, is called the person who is like a diamond. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. In the First Division, the Fifty-Ninth Discourse, "The Heap of Filth," is concluded.
The Discourse on Māra’s Domain.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
“Bhikkhus, possessing three qualities, a bhikkhu transcends Māra’s domain and shines forth like the sun.”
“By which three?

Here, monks, a monk is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, he is endowed with the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, and he is endowed with the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training.
Endowed with these three qualities, monks, a monk transcends the realm of Māra and shines forth like the sun.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“Virtue, concentration, and wisdom—”
He for whom these are well-developed,
having transcended the realm of Māra,
shines forth like the sun.
This matter too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The tenth [sutta].
The first chapter.
Its summary verse:
The root-element, then two kinds of feeling,
two kinds of seeking, and two kinds of taints.
They say that from craving and from the realm of Māra,
the first [fetter] is called "the group" (vagga) and the second is called "the released" (mutta).
